prompt_text:
For Mars, let's try a different approach to locations. (1) One mechanic is that "A + B in location P" behaves differently from just "A + B without a location" or "A + B in a different location". This will only be in places where it really makes sense that a combination requires a particular setting. In this way the location acts as a catalyst. (2) One mechanic is that a location itself acts as an element, hence "A + P" can produce a new element B. This new element can be placed anywhere and is no longer tied to the location. For instance if we drag "fire" element onto "glacier" location then we produce water. Note that neither A nor B nor the new element C are in any way tied to the location. You might say that element "C" is a portable encapsulation of some aspect of the location, having transmuted it in some way. (3) One mechanic is that an item has to be placed on a location to satisfy a victory condition. For instance if the goal is "put a receiver on the high ridge" then it is satisfied by dragging the receiver onto the high ridge.

In the current prototype it was doing something different with locations: it looked like (1) placements onto a location could be sticky so if I placed something there then it couldn't move away, (2) placements onto a location were cumulative so the location accumulated more than one item and they combined together. I don't want either. I didn't like the "accumulate more than one item" because it broke the central "A+B=C" premise of the game.

This means we have to be disciplined about the combined items. We can't say that a combined item is "heater+bed". The combined item has to be something recognizable and namable in its own right. It might be that the combined item is "heated bed". Likewise, we can't say that a combined item is "fork+spoon+plate" because that's not really a thing.

**My intermediate response**

The cosmic story has also been through a rewrite and fresh review. Its strongest proposed arc is: make a star, use its scattered material in a later solar system, grow rocky worlds and icy bodies, form Earth and the Moon, then descend to the surface as rain collects into a sea.

That keeps the raw-creation theme throughout. The remaining question is whether there are enough satisfying combinations between the big transformations, rather than too much watching time pass. We’re testing that on small paper boards before proposing any implementation.

**My subsequent draft**

The cosmic draft is ready to consider. Its working shape is **a star’s material becoming a sea**:

1. In the cooling early universe, combine light nuclei and electrons into hydrogen and helium gas.
2. Gather gas into a protostar, then feed it more gas to form a massive star.
3. Follow that star through its life and destruction. Its ejected material mixes into another cloud.
4. After further stellar generations, work with rock dust, metal grains and cold dust carrying reactive atoms. The Sun and its disk form around this material.
5. Assemble rocky clumps into growing worlds. Alongside that, make icy grains and water-rich bodies. These two threads share material and can be pursued in either order.
6. Follow young Earth and a smaller world into a Moon-forming collision. Earth survives; the debris becomes the Moon.
7. Follow the same Earth as it cools. Descend to its surface and combine rain with a rock basin: a sea, beneath the Moon.

The ending is the change of scale: something that began as particles and stars has become a place you could stand beside. I’d keep life for a separate continuation rather than tack on an oversimplified origin-of-life recipe.
